passage:
At the school fair in the hall, Ira opened her palm to show three coins. Aadhya opened hers: two. Her face crumpled.
"Ira has more! It is not fair!"
Mummy knelt beside her. "Aadhya, in our house pocket money goes up as you get older. Ira is older, so she has three now. When you reach her age you will have three too. And each of you decides what to spend or save."
Aadhya sniffled. "Can I save mine?"
"Of course."
Ira held out her hand. "Come and see the bangle stall with me?"

qa.q: How many coins did Aadhya have at the fair?
Why did Aadhya cry when she saw Ira's coins?
qa.a: She was hurt because she felt Ira was getting more, and she wanted the rule to be clear and fair.
She gave a clear rule based on age, promised the same for Aadhya later, and let each child choose how to spend or save.

qa.q: How might Ira see the moment?
qa.a: She seems kind and not gloating, since she invites Aadhya to the bangle stall after the crying.

grounding: A child cries because her sister has more pocket money; the family explains age-based rules and lets each child choose.

passage: On market day, Amma gave Deepika Didi five rupees and gave Tushar two. Tushar's face crumpled. "Didi got more! It's not fair!" He cried so loudly the goats looked up. Amma crouched down. "Didi is nine and you are five. In our house, older children get a bit more, because they buy their own pencils. When you are nine, you'll get the same." Tushar sniffed. "Every time?" "Every time. Same rule for everyone." "And I can choose what to do with mine?" "You choose." Tushar thought hard, then dropped one coin in his tin and kept one for a toffee.

qa.q: How much did Amma give Tushar?
Why did Tushar cry so loudly?
qa.a: He felt hurt and that it was unfair, because Didi got more and he didn't know why.

qa.q: What did Amma do to make the fairness clear?
qa.a: She explained an age-based rule that is the same for everyone, and let Tushar choose how to use his own coins.

qa.q: How might Deepika feel when Tushar cries?
qa.a: She may feel a bit awkward, but Amma's clear rule shows it isn't favouritism.

grounding: A young boy cries because his sister gets more pocket money, and his mother explains a clear age-based rule and lets him choose how to use his.

passage: On Friday in their Amman flat, Baba gave out pocket money. Leila got a big coin. Nour got a small one. Nour threw hers on the floor and cried. "Leila always gets more! You love her more!" Baba picked up the coin and sat Nour on his knee. "Leila is eight. You are five. When you're eight, you'll get the same. It's the rule for both of you, not because of love." "Promise?" "Promise. Let's write it on the fridge." Nour watched Baba draw two ladders with coins on each step. Then she chose to put her coin in the jar for stickers.

qa.q: What did Baba draw on the fridge?
qa.a: He drew two ladders with coins on each step.

qa.q: What was Nour worried about when she said "You love her more"?
qa.a: She felt hurt and worried that getting less money meant Baba loved Leila more.

qa.q: How did Baba prevent hidden hurt?
qa.a: He explained an age-based rule, made it visible on the fridge and let Nour choose how to use her own coin.

qa.q: What would change if Baba gave Leila more in secret?
qa.a: Nour might find out later and feel hurt and unloved, without knowing the reason.

grounding: A young girl cries that her older sister gets more pocket money, and her father explains a clear, visible age-based rule and lets her choose.
